beats.headline: The river was the road
beats.body: Bangkok to Chiang Mai took about three months upstream - a month of it working through [thirty-two rapids](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/63818). One documented journey, not an average. The Ping was vital, seasonal and difficult.

beats.headline: Trade is documented. A route is not.
beats.body: Mule caravans linked Chiang Mai into the trading world of southwest China. What cannot be drawn is a single road: routes shifted with politics, water, security and season, so this layer is a corridor, not a line.

beats.headline: Tarmac, on a different alignment
beats.body: Highway 11 reached the city from the south-east as the last section of the Superhighway. It did not pave a caravan trail; it is a separate layer of the network, drawn from [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright).

beats.headline: The line reached Chiang Mai
beats.body: The Northern Line arrived through the Khun Tan tunnel, 1,352 m long and eleven years in the digging. A three-month river journey became a timetable. Modern sources render the year as 1921 or 1922; the archive gives the Thai date, so we do too.

beats.headline: The connection with no route
beats.body: The airport opened in 1934. The city's first coworking space followed in 2013. Work now arrives from everywhere at once, and there is no line to draw for it - which is why this is where the past hands over.

hotspots.label: Chiang Mai railway station
hotspots.blurb: The national terminus, 1.57 km from here.
hotspots.body: The railway landed almost beside the older river-commercial landscape - the new connection on top of the old one.

hotspots.label: Khun Tan tunnel
hotspots.body: Dangerous and disease-prone. A frequently repeated toll of more than a thousand deaths has not been independently verified, and this piece does not repeat it as fact.

hotspots.label: Chiang Mai airport
hotspots.body: It joined the national airports authority on 1 March 1988 - a different event, often conflated with the opening.

beats.headline: Start here
beats.body: One point, on Wat Ket. Half of everyone alive is closer to it than you think.

beats.headline: How far to reach half the world
beats.body: A circle grows out from Wat Ket. At 1,000 km it holds four percent of the world's people; at 2,000 km, a fifth; at about 3,400 km, half. Counted from [GHS-POP](https://ghsl.jrc.ec.europa.eu/), the same field the columns are drawn from.

beats.headline: And then it stops growing
beats.body: The next three thousand kilometres add a sixth as much again. The circle that holds half of humanity is not much bigger than the one that holds a fifth.

hotspots.label: Wat Ket
hotspots.body: Moving the centre here from the mathematically best point costs almost nothing. Wat Ket is not near a centre of the world's population; it is one.

beats.headline: A generation that grew up here
beats.body: Imagine a hundred children conceived around Cosmo Local CNX in 2026, born in 2027, turning eighteen now. Call them Gen C. This is the city they grew up in.

beats.headline: How to drink from a river without drowning
beats.body: A fai is a weir. It does not hoard the river or block it; it slows the water and shares the flow through smaller channels, letting the rest run on. Every place on this map found its own fai.

beats.headline: Ban Tawan
beats.body: A front-porch shop just inside the eastern gate, in the shadow of the sunrise. The first Journeyfolk mark was issued here.

beats.headline: Lanna World School
beats.body: Forty-one children in a borrowed shed in Wat Ket. By 2034 a joint demonstration school of all eight universities in the city.
